evidence.statement: Most claims directly match the source: customer-support agents answer natural-language inquiries, personalized learning creates tailored quizzes and study guides, code generation produces snippets/functions/modules, and image generation creates visuals from text descriptions.
The q2 stem adds a potentially inaccurate workplace qualifier even though one keyed answer, creating study guides, is sourced to educational platforms rather than explicitly to workplace use.

The q2 correct set is ambiguous because the stem asks for workplace uses while the keyed option Creating study guides comes from the source's personalized-learning use case, not an explicitly workplace context.

Distractors generally represent neighboring source use cases or configuration concepts, such as marketing, visual generation, personalized learning, and TPM configuration, making them credible while remaining distinguishable under the scenarios.
Wrong options diagnose realistic category confusions, including support versus marketing, visuals versus learning, coding versus support, and generation versus deployment configuration.

The sequence moves from recognition and definition through understanding and then repeated workplace applications, but it briefly returns from the broad q2 recognition task to lower-level recall before building through the later application items.
The 13-item sequence alternates true/false, multi-select, fill-blank, arrange, single-choice, and application formats without long disruptive runs of one mechanic.
Several mechanics reuse nearly identical stems: Arrange the parts into a correct sentence appears in q4, q8, and q11, and Select all that apply recurs across q2, q7, q10, and q13.
The store support, differentiated-learning, web-app development, campaign mockup, and launch-copy scenarios resemble credible workplace or educational decisions grounded in the source use cases.

Many applied items give useful intrinsic and instructional feedback that names the correct category and the consequence of choosing a distractor, but q1 and q2 have comparatively terse explanations and q2 does not resolve its workplace-versus-education distinction.

The mix of basic definitions and straightforward application scenarios fits a Level 2 objective focused on identifying generative AI and matching it to common uses; the application items remain bounded by explicit source examples.

Core terms remain consistent with the source across the session, including natural language, artificial intelligence, personalized learning, virtual agent, image and video generation, and code snippets/functions/modules.

The session is source-grounded, varied, and generally instructive, with coherent coverage of major use cases; the main learner-facing weakness is the ambiguous q2 framing, compounded by repeated prompt templates.

largest_gap.summary: The q2 stem conflicts with one of its keyed answers by restricting the task to workplace uses while including an educational study-guide use case.

evidence.statement: The source describes creating study guides under personalized learning and tutoring for educational platforms, while q2 asks for workplace uses and keys Creating study guides as correct.

largest_gap.repair_instruction: Change only question_text to ask for common uses or applications of generative AI rather than workplace uses. Preserve question_type, options, correct_answer, and all other payload fields.

result.concise_summary: The session is largely source-faithful, varied, and appropriately scaffolded. One repairable ambiguity in q2 should be resolved by narrowing the stem to common applications rather than workplace uses.

rounds.repair_summary: Changed q2 question_text from workplace uses to common uses so the keyed study-guide answer is unambiguous.

metadata.unit_title: What generative AI can do · Level 2
metadata.unit_slo: Identify what generative AI is and match it to common workplace uses.

evidence.statement: The source assigns around-the-clock customer support to AI-powered virtual agents, personalized quizzes to learning platforms, and product/blog/social content to marketing use cases; the artifact preserves those distinctions in the false claim and applied items.

The multi-select items have clearly source-supported answer sets: marketing/customer-response/study-guide uses, personalized-learning outputs, and coding outputs are each separable from their distractors.

Distractors are drawn from neighboring source use cases or configuration concepts, such as marketing, visual generation, personalized learning, and TPM configuration, making them credible without fitting the stated task.
The artifact explicitly labels realistic confusions such as generation versus deployment configuration, support versus marketing, visuals versus writing, and learning versus support.

The ordered sequence moves from identifying generative AI and its uses to recalling key terms, arranging concepts, and applying use-case matches in customer support, learning, coding, visuals, and marketing.
The session uses true/false, multi-select, fill-in, sentence arrangement, and single-choice mechanics across the sequence; only the final two items repeat multiple choice consecutively.
The three arrange-sentence items use the identical prompt stem, “Arrange the parts into a correct sentence,” creating formulaic repetition even though their concepts differ.

The applied scenarios represent credible workplace or education decisions: after-hours customer support, learners progressing at different speeds, implementing a web feature, reviewing a campaign visual, and preparing launch copy.

Most applied items explain why the selected use fits and why distractors belong elsewhere; however, the incorrect intrinsic feedback for the first item, “A learning task would be assigned to support,” is vague and does not clearly state the governing distinction.
The Level 2 session combines foundational recall items with later Applying items, including contextual decisions about support, learning, coding, visual generation, and marketing.

The artifact consistently uses source terminology including generative AI, artificial intelligence, natural language, virtual agents, personalized learning, image and video generation, Copilot, and code snippets/functions/modules.

The exact sequence is source-faithful, varied across use cases and mechanics, and generally moves from recognition to application; repeated arrangement wording and one weak feedback phrase reduce polish.

largest_gap.summary: Three sentence-arrangement items repeat the same prompt stem verbatim.

evidence.statement: The prompt text is identical across the personalized-learning, code-generation, and marketing-content arrangement items.

largest_gap.repair_instruction: Rewrite only the question_text for these three items so each arrangement prompt has a distinct, source-bounded stem; preserve question_type, word_bank, correct_order, answers, and feedback.
